Unfolding, $\maj(s) = \true$ iff $2\,\ones(s) > n$. Using
$\errors(s,\true) = n - \ones(s)$, the condition $2\,\ones(s) > n$ is equivalent
to $2(n - \ones(s)) < n$, i.e.\ $2\,\errors(s,\true) < n$. Both directions follow
by linear arithmetic.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Asymmetry of the biconditional]
The analogous biconditional for $b = \false$ is \emph{false}. The forward
implication $2\,\errors(s,\false) < n \Rightarrow \maj(s) = \false$ holds by
Theorem~\ref{thm:correct}, but its converse fails at the exact tie
$2\,\errors(s,\false) = n$: there the decoder correctly outputs \false{} (the
strict $>$ tie-break favors \false) even though exactly half the readouts are
corrupted. Hence the clean iff is available only for the \true{} codeword. This
is the precise consequence of the tie-break convention.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[Tightness of the $n/2$ threshold,
\texttt{majority\_threshold\_tight}]
\label{thm:tight}
For every $k \geq 1$, on length $n = 2k$ there exists a readout
$s : \Fin\,(2k) \to \Bool$ with
\[

\]
\end{theorem}

Define $s(i) = \true$ if $i < k$ and $s(i) = \false$ if $i \geq k$. The positions
with $s(i) = \false$ are exactly $\{k, \dots, 2k-1\}$, of cardinality $k$; these
are the corrupted positions relative to $b = \true$, so $\errors(s,\true) = k$
(formally via the bijection $i \mapsto i + k$). Moreover $\ones(s) = k$, so
$2\,\ones(s) = 2k = n \not> n$, whence $\maj(s) = \false \neq \true$.
\end{proof}

the exact correctness radius: every weight strictly below $n/2$ is corrected, and
weight exactly $n/2$ (for even $n$) admits a failure. Theorem~\ref{thm:tight}
also certifies non-vacuity of the guarantee.

\section{Persistent $H_0$: Definitions}

Fix a finite vertex type $V$ (the measurement outcomes). A binary relation
$r : V \to V \to \mathrm{Prop}$ encodes ``linked at a given proximity
threshold.'' Connected components are the equivalence classes of the equivalence
closure $\EqvGen(r)$---the smallest equivalence relation containing $r$, i.e.\
its reflexive--symmetric--transitive closure. The set of components is the
quotient $\Quot(\EqvGen(r))$.

\begin{definition}[Zeroth Betti number, \texttt{betti0}]
For a relation $r$ on $V$ with finite component quotient,
\[
  \beta_0(r) = \#\,\Quot\big(\EqvGen(r)\big),
\]
the number of connected components of $(V, r)$. Finiteness of the quotient is
taken as an explicit hypothesis (a quotient of a finite type need not admit a
computable decidable-equality structure), keeping the statement honest.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Component map, \texttt{componentMap}]
Let $r_1, r_2$ be relations on $V$ with $r_1 \subseteq r_2$ (i.e.\
$r_1(a,b) \Rightarrow r_2(a,b)$ for all $a, b$). The induced component map
\[
  \mathrm{componentMap}(r_1, r_2) : \Quot(\EqvGen(r_1)) \to \Quot(\EqvGen(r_2))
\]
sends the $r_1$-component of a vertex to its $r_2$-component. It is well-defined
because $\EqvGen$ is monotone in its base relation: $r_1 \subseteq r_2$ implies
$\EqvGen(r_1) \subseteq \EqvGen(r_2)$, so $r_1$-equivalent vertices remain
$r_2$-equivalent and the quotient map descends.
\end{definition}

A \emph{filtration step} is precisely such a refinement $r_1 \subseteq r_2$:
raising the proximity threshold can only add links.

\section{Persistent $H_0$: Main Results}

\begin{lemma}[Surjectivity of the component map,
\texttt{componentMap\_surjective}]
\label{lem:surj}
If $r_1 \subseteq r_2$, then $\mathrm{componentMap}(r_1, r_2)$ is surjective.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Let $y \in \Quot(\EqvGen(r_2))$. Since the quotient map is surjective, $y = [a]_{r_2}$
for some vertex $a$. Then
$\mathrm{componentMap}(r_1, r_2)([a]_{r_1}) = [a]_{r_2} = y$. Hence every
$r_2$-component is hit.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[$H_0$ persistence, \texttt{betti0\_persistence}]
\label{thm:persist}
If $r_1 \subseteq r_2$ on a finite vertex type $V$ (with both component quotients
finite), then
\[
  \beta_0(r_2) \leq \beta_0(r_1).
\]
The zeroth Betti number is monotone non-increasing along a filtration.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:surj} the component map is surjective. A surjection between
finite types forces the cardinality of the domain to be at least that of the
codomain, so
\[
  \beta_0(r_2) = \#\,\Quot(\EqvGen(r_2)) \leq \#\,\Quot(\EqvGen(r_1)) = \beta_0(r_1).
  \qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

Conceptually: adding links can only \emph{merge} components, never split them, so
their count cannot increase. This is the discrete birth/death structure of the
$H_0$ barcode.

\begin{theorem}[Non-degeneracy / merge witness, \texttt{componentMap\_merges}]
\label{thm:merge}
There is an explicit instance over $V = \Bool$, with relations
$r_1 \subsetneq r_2$, in which two distinct $r_1$-components are identified under
$r_2$; the component map is non-injective and a genuine merge occurs.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Discussion]
Take $r_1$ purely reflexive, so $\false$ and $\true$ lie in two components
($\beta_0(r_1) = 2$), and take $r_2$ to link $\false$ with $\true$, fusing them
($\beta_0(r_2) = 1$). The component map sends both $r_1$-components to the single
$r_2$-component, witnessing $\beta_0(r_2) = 1 < 2 = \beta_0(r_1)$ and certifying
that Theorem~\ref{thm:persist} is genuinely attained as a strict inequality.
\end{proof}

\section{The Bridge: One Phenomenon, Two Invariants}
\label{sec:bridge}

When a NISQ experiment is repeated, correct readouts agree and form a dominant
cluster while errors are scattered. Combinatorially this is the \emph{majority
class}; topologically it is the \emph{largest connected component} of the
proximity graph. On the logic side, error is the Hamming weight $\errors(s,b)$
and the decision boundary is $2\,\errors < n$
(Theorems~\ref{thm:correct}--\ref{thm:tight}). On the topology side, error
structure is read from $\beta_0$ and merging is the only dynamic
(Theorem~\ref{thm:persist}), with merges genuinely occurring
(Theorem~\ref{thm:merge}). A logical failure corresponds to a \emph{premature
merge}: the minority cluster fusing into the majority so as to flip the dominant
component's label. The survival time of the correct cluster---its $H_0$ bar
length---is the topological avatar of the Hamming margin $n - 2\,\errors$.

\section{Future Directions}

Each conjecture is falsifiable: provable, or disprovable by an explicit finite
counterexample.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{C1. Topological decoding equals Hamming-ball decoding below
threshold.} Define the topological decoder as the dominant
$\beta_0$-component of the proximity graph at the optimal threshold; for the
repetition code its output equals majority voting whenever $2\,\mathrm{err} < n$.
The largest connected component is exactly the majority class, so $H_0$ recovers
the combinatorial threshold of Theorem~\ref{thm:correct}. Both endpoints are
formalized; the missing link is a lemma identifying the dominant component with
the majority class.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{C2. Persistence monotonicity is strict iff a merge event
occurs.} For $r_1 \subseteq r_2$, $\beta_0(r_2) < \beta_0(r_1)$ iff there exist
$a, b$ that are $r_2$-connected but not $r_1$-connected. The component map is
non-injective exactly at a merge (Theorem~\ref{thm:merge} witnesses the forward
direction), converting the $\leq$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:persist} into a sharp
$</=$ dichotomy.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{C3. Error suppression rate is governed by the longest $H_0$
bar.} For independent bit-flip noise at rate $p < 1/2$, the logical error
probability decays as $\Theta(\exp(-c\,n))$, with $c$ determined by the expected
length of the longest $H_0$ bar of the random proximity filtration. A logical
failure is precisely a premature merge of the minority into the majority, so the
survival time of the correct component controls the suppression rate.
Theorem~\ref{thm:tight} pins the failure boundary; layering Chernoff/Hoeffding
concentration on the formalized combinatorics is the natural next step.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{C4. Filtration refinement never increases logical error.}
Refining the proximity filtration cannot increase the logical error rate,
mirroring Theorem~\ref{thm:persist} at the level of decoding outcomes.

\section{Conclusion}

We established two sharp invariants of NISQ majority-vote error mitigation: an
exact worst-case $n/2$ correctness threshold (Theorem~\ref{thm:correct}), a clean
biconditional for the \true{} codeword with a characterized failure of the
converse for \false{} (Theorem~\ref{thm:iff}), and a tightness witness
(Theorem~\ref{thm:tight}); on the topological side, monotone decay of $\beta_0$
along a filtration (Theorem~\ref{thm:persist}) with an explicit merge witness
(Theorem~\ref{thm:merge}). The two invariants are two readings of one
phenomenon---the survival of the majority cluster---and the conjectures of
Section~7 chart a path toward a noise-robust, topology-aware decoding theory.

  simpa [componentMap] using ha
